catalog_quote: The first point is the case of why (5), which also appears in the excerpt in a phonologically Zulu-integrated form wayi (7). The second form is marked by two traits: a lengthening of the first syllable of the word, according to Zulu prosody, which requires the penultimate syllable to be long; and an added vowel -i at the end of the word, which clearly sounds, and separates the question word from the next verbal phrase. The word appears in positions where one could expect the Zulu yini. ... [p.180:] Examples 7.23 and 7.24 show a particular way to use the borrowing one in White City: one is an adjective meaning 'alone' or 'by oneself' This meaning is not expressed by one in English, as the adjective would be alone. In Example 7.24, wani is pronounced with a long vowel -a-, in conformity with Zulu prosody, and the final vowel -i is pronounced distinctly.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Iscamtho in White City is spoken on a Soweto-Zulu base whose prosody applies: the penultimate syllable of the word is lengthened (the Nguni penultimate prominence), and borrowings integrated into Zulu (why > wayi, one > wani) receive this penultimate length. The base is tonal (low tone marks the copulative noun prefix, p.108).
new_statements.exceptions: Unintegrated English/Afrikaans borrowings keep source-language phonology (p.5/316: 'English borrowings feature English phonology'); no other exceptions discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level penultimate vowel length inherited from the Zulu base language; the remark is incidental (about loanword integration), not a dedicated prosody description. Iscamtho is treated by the author as a slang lexicon/style on a mixed Soweto Zulu base, so its prosody is that of the base language (Zulu; Sotho-based Iscamtho would follow Sotho).
new_statements.identity_note: Aycard 2014 describes Iscamtho as used in White City-Jabavu, Soweto, on a (mixed) Soweto Zulu base; the prosodic remark is explicitly about 'Zulu prosody' applying to local speech, i.e. the base language (Zulu, zulu1248). Camtho/Iscamtho [cmt] is a register/lexicon (Glottolog family 'Speech Register'), so any stress property is inherited from the base language (Zulu- or Sotho-based varieties differ). Hurst 2008 concerns Cape Town tsotsitaal (Xhosa/Afrikaans base), a different variety.
